Education & Research

Breast Enlargement FAQs: 15 Questions Answered

Straightforward answers to the questions patients most often ask. Every individual situation still requires assessment by an appropriately qualified clinician.

Home/Education & Research/Breast Enlargement FAQs: 15 Questions Answered

These answers are general information

They cannot replace an assessment by a qualified clinician who can review your health, anatomy and expectations in person.

Common questions

Breast enlargement FAQs

Some products and procedures are marketed for this, but evidence that they reliably and lastingly increase breast volume is limited or absent. Weight gain can increase breast size because breasts contain fat, but this is not targeted or controllable. See breast enlargement without surgery.

No. Injections and threads can cause infection, lumps, tissue damage and complications that are hard to treat. “Non-surgical” describes the method, not the level of risk.

Implants are not lifetime devices. Many people need further surgery at some point. See our page on how long implants last.

It is possible. Reasons include rupture, scar tissue tightening, changes in breast shape or size preference, and implant displacement. See breast revision surgery.

Both have a silicone shell. Saline implants are filled with sterile salt water; silicone implants contain a cohesive gel. They differ in feel, appearance and how a rupture is detected. See silicone vs saline implants.

Many people can, but it depends on the incision, implant placement and your breast tissue. Discuss this before surgery. See pregnancy and breastfeeding.

They can make imaging more complex. Tell the imaging team you have implants so they can adapt the technique. See implants and mammograms.

Fat that survives in its new location can last, but a portion is usually reabsorbed, and the amount varies between people. See how much fat survives.

It varies by procedure and person. Many people return to light activity within days to weeks, with restrictions on strenuous exercise lasting longer. Your surgeon’s instructions take priority. See breast augmentation.

No. Photos show one person’s result under particular conditions and cannot predict yours.

It is liquid silicone or other substances injected directly into tissue. It is not the same as a regulated implant and can cause permanent harm, including lumps, migration and chronic inflammation. See unsafe breast injections.

Check medical registration, specialist training, experience with your specific procedure, and the facility’s emergency arrangements. See how to check credentials.

Some surgeons advise waiting, because pregnancy and breastfeeding change breast shape. This is a personal decision to discuss with your surgeon.

Fever, spreading redness, sudden one-sided swelling, severe pain, wound opening, chest pain or breathlessness need prompt medical attention. See urgent warning signs.

Not necessarily. Proportion, tissue quality and long-term risk matter more than volume alone. See choosing implant size.
